newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK ends probe on disgraced aide,but questions stay.
newsitem.headline: HK ends probe on disgraced aide,but questions stay.

text.p: Hong Kong on Wednesday closed the book on a a marathon inquiry into the disgraced chief of the colony's immigration service but left crucial questions hanging.

The abrupt departure of former immigration director Laurence Leung raised a storm of speculation which forced Hong Kong's civil service chief to step in at one point and publicly dismiss rumours that Leung was a Chinese spy.

"There is no evidence and no reason to suppose that Mr Leung is or was a Chinese agent," Chief Secretary Anson Chan, number two in the colonial administration to Governor Chris Patten, told a Legislative Council panel of enquiry probing the case back in January.
The government had originally insisted Leung stood down for personal reasons but later conceded the 55-year-old bureaucrat had failed an integrity check.

Leung's post was highly sensitive because he had authority over immigration, nationality and frontier affairs, as well as access to confidential information on citizens, which carries strong security implications ahead of Chinese rule from June 30.

Some panelists had doubted that the government's reasons for forcing Leung to retire -- that he concealed business dealings and violated repayment terms on a government home loan -- were enough to justify his instant removal last July.

The government nevertheless refused to release confidential details about his dismissal, saying the information would harm "public interest" and compromise future personal vetting activities conducted by Hong Kong's powerful graft-busting commission.

Panel members who wound up the eight month enquiry on Wednesday said they were satisfied with the reasons for the government's decision to force Leung's resignation but complained crucual questions had been unanswered.

"Government officials had tailored their evidence and withheld material information to mislead the Legislative Council and the public into accepting an account of Mr Leung's departure from government service which they know to be untrue," panel chairman Ip Kwok-him told a news conference.
"It was like getting blood from stone," he added.
Panel member Selina Chow acknowledged certain subjects remained off limits.
"Obviously there are certain areas where we were somehow constrained. People ask about political motives, we cannot say that we have been equipped to investigate into that," said Chow.
